::: {.lead}
After the vectors, matrices and transformations of lectures 1–14 (revised
in lecture 15), the second part of the course gave you the tools for
**decisions** and **chance** in games: logic for rules and doors,
probability for dice and drops, random numbers and seeds, and the balance
and fairness that players feel. Lectures 26–28 joined everything in
applied problems: a moving object and a random level (@fig-map). In this
revision lesson you go through the second part once more. Each section
gives the **key facts**, one **mixed example** from a game, the most
**common mistake**, and a short task. The last section shows how to
**present** a solution, because in this lesson you also present one
problem to the class. The mini-game at the end takes you past all parts.
:::

## Key terms

## 29.1 Logic and truth tables (lectures 16–17)

::: {.callout-important title="Key facts 29.1 — Propositions and tables"}
- A **proposition** is true (T, 1) or false (F, 0). In code: a `bool`.
- ¬p (NOT), p ∧ q (AND: both), p ∨ q (OR: at least one), p ⊕ q (XOR:
  exactly one), p → q (IF–THEN: false only when p is T and q is F;
  $p \to q \equiv \neg p \vee q$).
- **Precedence:** NOT, then AND, then OR, then IF–THEN; brackets first.
- A **truth table** with n variables has $2^n$ rows. A **tautology** is
  true in every row; two propositions are **equivalent** when their last
  columns are equal.
- From a table back to a rule: **one AND per true row**, joined with OR.
:::

![A truth table, column by column (lecture 17).](../week-09/images/tt-steps.png){#fig-tt width=90%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 29.1 — The chest of Torch Hall"}
The chest opens when $(k \vee c) \wedge \neg t$: the player has the key k
or the code c, and the trap t is off.

1. The table has $2^3 = 8$ rows.
2. With k = F, c = T, t = F: $(F \vee T) \wedge \neg F = T \wedge T = T$:
   the chest opens.
3. The true rows are (k, c) = (T, T), (T, F), (F, T), each with t = F:
   **3 rows**, so 3 test cases must open the chest and 5 must not.
:::

{{< sim file="../week-09/sims/truth-table-lab.html" poster="../week-09/sims/truth-table-lab.png" title="Truth Table Lab: every case of a condition" height="700" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Reading $p \wedge q \vee r$ as $p \wedge (q \vee r)$. AND comes before OR,
so it means $(p \wedge q) \vee r$. When in doubt, write the brackets.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Two tables"}
1. Build the truth tables of $p \to q$ and of $\neg p \vee q$. Are they
   equivalent?
2. In **Truth Table Lab**, find the true rows of a condition with three
   variables.

*Your result:* two tables and one sentence.
:::

## 29.2 Boolean algebra and game rules (lectures 18–19)

::: {.callout-important title="Key facts 29.2 — Laws and rules"}
- With 1 and 0: $\neg p = 1 - p$, $p \wedge q = p \cdot q$,
  $p \vee q = p + q$ (with 1 + 1 = 1).
- Laws: identity, domination, complement ($p \wedge \neg p \equiv F$),
  distributive, absorption ($p \vee (p \wedge q) \equiv p$).
- **De Morgan:** $\neg(p \wedge q) \equiv \neg p \vee \neg q$ and
  $\neg(p \vee q) \equiv \neg p \wedge \neg q$.
- A **decision table** has $2^n$ rows, one action each: complete, no
  conflicts. In an **else-if chain**, the first true rule wins; a rule that
  the rules above catch completely is **unreachable**.
- **Edge cases** for "health < 30": test 29, 30 and 31.
:::

![De Morgan's laws (lecture 18).](../week-09/images/de-morgan.png){#fig-dm width=90%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 29.2 — A long rule and a guard"}
1. Simplify $\neg(\neg a \vee b) \vee (a \wedge b)$. De Morgan:
   $(a \wedge \neg b) \vee (a \wedge b)$. Distributive:
   $a \wedge (\neg b \vee b)$. Complement and identity: **a**.
2. A guard has `if (health < 30) Flee(); else if (health < 10) Hide();`.
   Every health below 10 is also below 30, so `Hide` is **unreachable**.
   Put the more specific rule (< 10) first.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Moving a NOT into brackets without swapping the operator:
$\neg(p \vee q)$ is **not** $\neg p \vee \neg q$. The NOT goes in, and OR
becomes AND.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Simplify and order"}
1. Simplify $\neg(p \wedge \neg q)$ with De Morgan, and name each law.
2. Write the edge cases for the rule "shield on when energy ≥ 50".

*Your result:* a short condition and three test values.
:::

## 29.3 Probability and expected value (lectures 20–21)

::: {.callout-important title="Key facts 29.3 — Chance and average"}
- Equally likely outcomes: $P(A) = \dfrac{|A|}{|S|}$;
  $P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A)$. Two steps with m and k outcomes give
  m × k pairs (a grid or a tree).
- $P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B)$. Independent:
  $P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)$.
- **Conditional:** $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \text{ and } B)}{P(B)}$;
  in general $P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \cdot P(B \mid A)$.
- **Expected value:** $E(X) = x_1 p_1 + x_2 p_2 + \dots$; a game is
  **fair** when E(win) − price = 0; the average number of tries until a
  success is $1/p$.
:::

![A tree diagram (lecture 20).](../week-10/images/tree.png){#fig-tree width=90%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 29.3 — Tokens and a dice stand"}
1. A chest on the raft holds 2 gold and 3 wood tokens. The player draws two
   without putting them back. $P(\text{both gold}) = \dfrac{2}{5} \cdot \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1}{10}$.
2. A dice stand costs 2 coins; a 6 wins 6 coins, all else nothing.
   $E(\text{win}) = 6 \cdot \dfrac{1}{6} = 1$, so the expected gain is
   1 − 2 = **−1 coin**: not fair. A fair price is 1 coin.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Multiplying the first chance twice for draws **without** putting back:
$\frac{2}{5} \cdot \frac{2}{5}$ is wrong. After one gold token is gone,
only 1 of 4 tokens is gold.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Two dice"}
1. Find P(sum ≥ 10) for two dice with a grid.
2. Find P(double | sum ≥ 10).

*Your result:* two fractions.
:::

## 29.4 Random numbers and distributions (lectures 22–23)

::: {.callout-important title="Key facts 29.4 — Generators and weights"}
- A **PRNG** computes each number from the one before. **LCG:**
  $x_{n+1} = (a \cdot x_n + c) \bmod m$; the first value is the **seed**.
  The same seed gives the same numbers.
- From $0 \le r < 1$: an integer = floor(r · (max − min)) + min; yes with
  probability p when r < p. `Random.Range(1, 7)` gives 1 … 6: the max is
  excluded for integers. **Seed once.**
- **Uniform:** every value equally likely. **Weighted:**
  $P(i) = \dfrac{w_i}{\sum w}$; pick with the cumulative weights.
- Sums of random numbers are **bell-shaped**; a random point in a circle
  needs radius $R\sqrt{r}$.
:::

![Weighted random choice (lecture 23).](../week-12/images/weighted.png){#fig-weighted width=90%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 29.4 — The daily cave and the loot"}
1. LCG with a = 5, c = 3, m = 16 and seed 7: $x_1 = 38 \bmod 16 = 6$,
   $x_2 = 33 \bmod 16 = 1$, $x_3 = 8 \bmod 16 = 8$. All players with seed 7
   get the same cave.
2. Loot weights: common 70, rare 25, epic 5 (sum 100). P(epic) = 0.05.
   Cumulative: 70, 95, 100. A draw r = 93.4 lies between 70 and 95:
   **rare**.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
`Random.Range(1, 6)` for a die: with integers it gives only 1 … 5. Use
`Random.Range(1, 7)`. And seeding again every frame with the time gives
the same number many times.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · A loot table"}
1. Weights 50, 30, 15, 5. Find each probability and the cumulative
   weights.
2. Which item does r = 81 give?

*Your result:* four probabilities and one item.
:::

## 29.5 Balance, fairness and generation (lectures 24, 25 and 28)

::: {.callout-important title="Key facts 29.5 — Balance and fairness"}
- **At least one** drop in n tries: $1 - (1 - p)^n$. For a share q of the
  players: $n \ge \dfrac{\ln(1 - q)}{\ln(1 - p)}$.
- A **pity timer** limits the longest wait. **Expected attacks** to win:
  hits needed ÷ hit chance.
- Independent tries have **streaks**, and no memory: the **gambler's
  fallacy** expects a result to be "due". A **shuffle bag** keeps the
  shares exact; **PRD** raises the chance with every miss.
- **Generation:** the same seed gives the same level; **rejection
  sampling** needs $1/p$ draws on average; a **flood fill** checks that the
  exit can be reached; test the generator with many seeds.
:::

![At least one drop in n tries (lecture 24).](../week-12/images/at-least-one.png){#fig-atleast width=90%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 29.5 — A rare pearl"}
1. A pearl drops with p = 0.05. In 20 dives:
   $1 - 0.95^{20} \approx 1 - 0.36 = 0.64$, not 100 %.
2. With a shuffle bag of 1 pearl in 20 dives, every player gets exactly one
   pearl in each full bag, and the longest wait is $2(20 - 1) = 38$ dives.
3. The generator places the pearl on a free tile by rejection sampling; a
   quarter of the tiles are free, so it needs 1 / 0.25 = **4 draws** on
   average.
:::

{{< sim file="../week-13/sims/bag-lab.html" poster="../week-13/sims/bag-lab.png" title="Bag Lab: pure random, shuffle bag or PRD?" height="660" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"20 tries at 5 % make 100 %." Chances of tries do not add up: use the
complement, $1 - (1 - p)^n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Drops and bags"}
1. p = 0.2: find P(at least one in 5 tries), and the number of tries for
   90 % of the players.
2. In **Bag Lab**, compare the longest drought of pure random and of a
   shuffle bag.

*Your result:* a probability, a number of tries and two droughts.
:::

## 29.6 Solving and presenting a mixed problem (lectures 26–27)

::: {.callout-important title="Key facts 29.6 — Solve, then present"}
- **Five steps** (lecture 26): read (given and asked), draw, choose the
  tool, compute with units, check.
- **Present** the solution in the same order (@fig-present): the
  **problem** in one sentence, the **sketch**, the **tool** and why, the
  **steps**, and the **check and answer** in game words.
- About one minute for each part. Speak to the class, not to the board;
  show one number check (a probability between 0 and 1, a sensible size).
- Listen to the other solutions: ask one question about the tool or the
  check.
:::

![Presenting a solution in five parts.](images/present-solution.png){#fig-present width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 29.6 — The pearl, presented"}
1. *Problem:* "A pearl drops with p = 0.1. After how many dives do 90 % of
   the players have one?"
2. *Sketch and tool:* a table of n and $1 - 0.9^n$; the "at least once"
   formula of lecture 24.
3. *Steps:* $n \ge \ln 0.1 / \ln 0.9 \approx 21.9$, so n = 22.
4. *Check and answer:* $1 - 0.9^{22} \approx 0.90$. "After 22 dives, nine
   of ten players have a pearl."
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Showing only the final number. The class cannot follow or check it.
Name the tool, show the steps, and say the answer as a sentence about the
game.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Present one problem"}
A chest has the weights 6, 3 and 1 (common, rare, epic), worth 10, 40 and
200 coins. Find the expected coins per chest, and prepare a five-part
presentation of your solution. Present it to the class (alone, about four
minutes).

*Your result:* a solution in five parts and one presentation.
:::

## Case study: Lucky Raft Finals

*Lucky Raft Finals* is a made-up revision game: the raft sails past eight
islands, one for each idea of lectures 16–28. The problems: a dock gate
with AND and NOT, a sailing rule with De Morgan, a sum of two dice, a
bonus when the first die is a 6, the expected coins of a crate, one step
of an LCG, a pearl in two dives, and a shot after four misses. The Game
challenge of the interactive lesson uses these problems. In the mini-game
below you sail past the islands.

{{< sim file="sims/raft-finals.html" poster="sims/raft-finals.png" title="Lucky Raft Finals: eight islands, eight ideas" kind="game" height="560" >}}

## Further reading

Rosen, *Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications*, 8th ed., Chapter 1
(logic) and Chapter 7 (probability). Schreiber and Romero, *Game Balance*
(2021), the chapters on probability and randomness.

## Exercises

1. Is "Open the gate!" a proposition? Why?
2. p = T and q = F. Find the values of p → q and of ¬p ∨ q.
3. How many rows has the truth table of a rule with 3 conditions?
4. Write ¬(a ∧ b) with De Morgan.
5. Simplify p ∨ (p ∧ q), and name the law.
6. `if (hp < 50) A(); else if (hp < 20) B();` Which rule is unreachable?
   Which edge cases test the first rule?
7. Two dice: find P(sum = 4).
8. One die: find P(not a 6).
9. A bag has 3 red and 1 blue token. Two draws without putting back: find
   P(both red).
10. A crate gives 0 coins with probability 0.5, 20 coins with 0.4 and 100
    coins with 0.1. Find the expected coins.
11. LCG $x_{n+1} = (5x_n + 3) \bmod 16$ with seed 7: find $x_1$.
12. Which values does `Random.Range(0, 4)` give with integers?
13. Two items have the weights 8 and 2. Find P(second item).
14. Drop rate 0.2, three tries: find P(at least one drop).
15. A 25 % critical hit missed five times in a row; the rolls are
    independent. What is the chance of a crit on the next roll?
16. Rejection sampling: one fifth of the candidates is allowed. How many
    draws are needed on average?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. No: it is an order, neither true nor false.
2. Both are F.
3. $2^3 = 8$.
4. ¬a ∨ ¬b.
5. p (absorption).
6. B (every hp < 20 is also < 50); test 49, 50, 51.
7. 3/36 = 1/12.
8. 5/6.
9. 3/4 · 2/3 = 1/2.
10. 0 + 8 + 10 = 18 coins.
11. 38 mod 16 = 6.
12. 0, 1, 2, 3.
13. 2/10 = 0.2.
14. 1 − 0.8³ = 1 − 0.512 = 0.488.
15. 25 %: independent rolls have no memory.
16. 5.
:::
